newsitem.title: UK: US rate rise to boost demand for dollar Eurobonds.
newsitem.headline: US rate rise to boost demand for dollar Eurobonds.

text.p: Demand for dollar Eurobonds was expected to pick up after the Easter holiday as investors sought to lock in higher coupons following the rise in U.S. interest rates, bankers said on Wednesday.
"Rates are higher and so are coupons, and we will see quite a good bid from retail investors (in the coming weeks)," a syndicate manager at a European bank said.
"There is also a strong bid on the institutional side, from Asia especially, due to the strong dollar," he said.

On Tuesday the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised the target for the fed funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. The move, the first U.S. rate rise for over two years, was taken as a pre-emptive measure to head off inflation.
"With the Fed having increased rates by only 25 b.p., expectations are there will be more increases to come," a trader at another European bank said.

"But there will be a period of stabilisation (in the primary market) for the month of April. As long as economic figures are not too worrying, people will make use of these levels and probably extend their maturity profile," he said.

The international bond market has already seen record issuance levels in the first quarter, with nearly $200 billion equivalent raised compared with $185 billion in the same period last year, Capital DATA Bondware figures showed.
Dollar bonds totalled $80 billion, up from $66 billion in the first quarter of 1996.
The 10-year dollar sector in particular was expected to see supply in the coming weeks, although an expensive repo market could curtail volumes to some extent.
"A lot of investors have been lengthening duration already because with low inflation and rising rates you would expect the yield curve to remain flat or flatten further," a U.S. bank trader said.

"The only problem has been the very tight 10-year repo market which has made it unattractive for dealers to be long 10-year bonds, and attractive for investors to hold Treasuries rather than Eurobonds," he said.
The market will watch to see whether the U.S. decides to auction a new 10-year bond or add to existing paper as this will impact repos, he said.
"As long as U.S. inflation remains under control and growth is healthy we would expect institutions to eye the 10-year dollar sector," the trader said.
On the retail side bankers expected three-, four- and five-year dollar bonds to surface, with the two-year sector unlikely to be very active.
"Swap spreads have moved out a bit after the rate hike which will help meet funding targets in the short-dated dollar sector," a swap trader at a European bank said.
At 1415 GMT the three-year swap spread was trading at 24 22 b.p., widening out by a pip a year to five years.
